prompt: Two routers use OSPFv2 on the same broadcast subnet. Which two interface parameters must match for a neighbor to form? (Choose two.)
options: Local OSPF process ID
Hello and dead intervals
OSPF router ID
OSPF area ID
Configured interface bandwidth
explanation: Hello and dead intervals and the area ID must match, along with the subnet and any authentication.

whyWrong.0: The process ID is local.
whyWrong.2: Router IDs must be unique, not identical.
whyWrong.4: Bandwidth affects cost, not neighbor formation.

exhibit.title: Representative Cisco syslog content
exhibit.text:
%LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface Gi0/1, changed state to down
%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Gi0/1, changed state to down

prompt: What do the 3 and 5 identify in these Cisco message headers?
options: Transport facility numbers assigned to the two receivers
Severity codes for critical and warning messages respectively
Severity codes for error and notification messages respectively
Sequence numbers used to reorder the messages at the server
explanation: The number between the Cisco component and the mnemonic is the severity: 3 is error and 5 is notification. LINK and LINEPROTO are components, not the transport facility.

whyWrong.0: The transport facility is encoded separately in the syslog PRI.
whyWrong.1: Critical is 2 and warning is 4.
whyWrong.3: These are severity numbers, not sequence numbers.

prompt: Port security is newly enabled on a static access port on Catalyst IOS, with no optional values changed. Which two defaults apply? (Choose two.)
options: Sticky learning is automatically enabled
Maximum secure MAC addresses is one
The switchport remains dynamic auto
Violation mode is restrict without shutdown
Violation mode is shutdown
explanation: The default maximum is one secure MAC address and the default violation mode is shutdown.

whyWrong.0: Sticky learning needs its own command.
whyWrong.2: Port security needs a static access or trunk mode, not dynamic auto.
whyWrong.3: Restrict must be configured explicitly.

prompt: Which description correctly identifies the interfaces value in the displayed JSON?
options: An object containing two unquoted member names
A string containing two comma-separated interface values
A Boolean value because each status is either up or down
An array whose elements are two interface objects
explanation: Square brackets make `interfaces` an array, and each pair of braces is an object. The up/down values are strings, not Booleans.

whyWrong.0: The value starts with a bracket, not a brace.
whyWrong.1: It is structured JSON, not a quoted string.
whyWrong.2: The status values are strings.

prompt: For IOS management AAA, which protocol and transport support per-command authorization?
options: Classic RADIUS over UDP 1812
TACACS+ over TCP 49
Classic RADIUS accounting over UDP 1813
TACACS+ over UDP 49
explanation: TACACS+ over TCP 49 separates authentication, authorization and accounting, so it supports per-command authorization.

whyWrong.0: RADIUS on UDP 1812 is authentication and does not provide per-command authorization.
whyWrong.2: UDP 1813 is RADIUS accounting.
whyWrong.3: TACACS+ uses TCP, not UDP.

prompt: SW1 uses LACP passive on otherwise compatible member ports. Which SW2 mode initiates the protocol needed to form that bundle?
options: passive
desirable
active
auto
explanation: LACP active initiates and passive responds. Desirable and auto are PAgP modes.

whyWrong.0: Two passive ends have no initiator.
whyWrong.1: Desirable is PAgP.
whyWrong.3: Auto is PAgP and does not answer LACP.

prompt: An ordinary Ethernet host's gateway should be on its local subnet. Which displayed setting is inconsistent?
options: The host address is the subnet broadcast address
The configured gateway lies outside the host’s /22
The subnet mask must be /16 because the address begins 172.16
The host and gateway have the same IPv4 address
explanation: 172.16.47.250/22 is in 172.16.44.0 to 172.16.47.255, so usable hosts end at .47.254. The gateway is outside that range.

whyWrong.0: The broadcast address is 172.16.47.255.
whyWrong.2: The configured mask applies, not a classful assumption.
whyWrong.3: The host and gateway addresses differ.

spec.title: VLAN 10 · Rapid PVST+
spec.caption: SW1 is root; the labeled short-method costs are authoritative for this calculation.

prompt: SW1 is the root. Using the explicitly shown path costs, which SW3 interface becomes the root port?
options: Fa0/24, because one hop always beats two
Gi0/1, because SW2’s MAC overrides root cost
Gi0/1, because the path through SW2 costs 8
Fa0/24, because its displayed number is lower
explanation: SW3 adds its Gi0/1 cost of 4 to SW2's root cost of 4, for 8. The direct link costs 19, so Gi0/1 is the root port.

whyWrong.0: STP does not use hop count.
whyWrong.1: The bridge ID matters only after equal cost.
whyWrong.3: Port number matters only after equal cost.

prompt: Under ordinary destination-based forwarding, which next hop is selected for 10.1.3.77 from these installed routes?
options: 10.9.9.2 because the static route has lower AD
10.9.9.1 because its OSPF metric is lower
203.0.113.1 because it is the default gateway
10.9.9.3 because the matching /26 is longest
explanation: 10.1.3.77 falls in 10.1.3.64/26, the longest matching route. Administrative distance compares sources for the same prefix, so it does not override a more specific route.

whyWrong.0: AD compares sources for the same prefix.
whyWrong.1: The /16 is less specific despite its metric.
whyWrong.2: The default route is used only when nothing more specific matches.

exhibit.title: Representative R1 NAT configuration
exhibit.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
 ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.252
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1 overload
access-list 1 permit 10.10.10.0 0.0.0.255

prompt: Client packets enter Gi0/0/0 and leave Gi0/0/1 in an inside-source PAT design. Routes and filtering are correct. Which missing setting stops the translation?
options: ip nat outside on GigabitEthernet0/0/1
ip nat outside on GigabitEthernet0/0/0
A permit for 203.0.113.0/30 in source ACL 1
A pool statement replacing interface overload
explanation: The egress interface lacks `ip nat outside`. Add it and test fresh traffic.

whyWrong.1: Gi0/0/0 is the correct inside interface.
whyWrong.2: The source ACL selects client addresses, not the outside address.
whyWrong.3: Interface overload is valid PAT and needs no pool.

prompt: Build ACL 110 to deny Telnet from 192.168.10.0/24 to 10.0.0.5 and permit everything else, with the deny first. Which two entries are needed? (Choose two.)
options: access-list 110 permit ip any any
access-list 110 permit tcp any any eq 23
explanation: The deny matches the source /24, destination host and TCP port 23. The final `permit ip any any` allows all other traffic.

whyWrong.1: ACLs use wildcard masks, not subnet masks.
whyWrong.3: `deny ip` also blocks other services to the host.
whyWrong.4: Permitting only Telnet leaves other traffic to the implicit deny.

prompt: The remote DHCP server 10.0.0.10 has the right VLAN 20 pool and return route, but R1 Gi0/0.20 has no relay. Which addition fits?
options: ip helper-address 10.0.0.10 on Gi0/0.20
ip helper-address 10.0.0.10 on the server-facing interface
default-router 10.0.0.10 in a new local DHCP pool
ip address 10.0.0.10 on the VLAN 20 subinterface
explanation: Configure the helper on the interface that receives the client broadcast. It relays to the server and supplies the relay address used for pool selection.

whyWrong.1: The server-facing interface does not receive the client broadcast.
whyWrong.2: A new local pool changes the design.
whyWrong.3: The server's address on the subinterface creates an addressing fault.

exhibit.title: Representative R2 HSRP brief
exhibit.text:
P indicates configured to preempt
Interface Grp Pri P State    Active     Standby Virtual IP
Gi0/0     1   150   Standby 10.1.1.1   local   10.1.1.254

prompt: R1 became active at priority 100 before R2 joined. R2 shows priority 150 and no P flag. Why is R2 standby?
options: The lower IP address must remain active in every HSRP group
Priority 150 is outside the supported HSRP range
R1’s router ID overrides the HSRP priority comparison
R2 has not been configured to preempt the existing active router
explanation: Without preemption, a higher-priority router does not take over a healthy active router. The missing P flag shows preemption is off.

whyWrong.0: The lower IP address does not always win.
whyWrong.1: 150 is a valid priority.
whyWrong.2: A router ID does not decide HSRP roles.

prompt: Three nearby 2.4 GHz APs use 20 MHz channels 1, 4 and 8, and a survey confirms overlap. Which plan reduces it while keeping three 20 MHz cells?
options: Put all three APs on channel 6 at maximum power
Use channels 1,6,11 with survey-appropriate power
Change the middle AP to a bonded 40 MHz channel
Keep channels 1,4,8 and increase all transmit powers
explanation: Channels 1, 6 and 11 are the standard non-overlapping 2.4 GHz plan.

whyWrong.0: One shared channel means shared airtime.
whyWrong.2: A wider channel uses more of a limited band.
whyWrong.3: More power does not remove overlap.

prompt: Build a link-local address with prefix FE80::/64 and a modified EUI-64 IID from MAC 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. Which is correct?
options: FE80::21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
FE80::1A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
FE80::1A2B:3CFF:FE4D:5E00
explanation: Insert FF:FE in the middle of the MAC and flip the U/L bit of the first octet, giving 021A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E.

whyWrong.1: This does not flip the U/L bit.
whyWrong.2: This omits FF:FE.
whyWrong.3: This rearranges the MAC bytes.

exhibit.title: Representative authoritative answer and change record
exhibit.text:
portal.example.test. 300 IN A 192.0.2.15
Approved new web address: 192.0.2.25
HTTP to 192.0.2.25: expected page

prompt: The authoritative answer for portal.example.test is shown, and the web server moved to 192.0.2.25. Which record needs correcting?
options: The MX record naming the mail exchanger
The PTR record used only for reverse lookup
The NS record naming the authoritative servers
The A record still pointing at the previous IPv4 address
explanation: The A record gives the IPv4 address for a forward lookup. Fix it, then allow for TTL caching.

whyWrong.0: MX names a mail exchanger.
whyWrong.1: PTR is for reverse lookups.
whyWrong.2: The evidence shows wrong answer data, not wrong delegation.

prompt: A play targets IOS devices over network_cli. Which task gathers the IPv4 routing table without changing configuration?
options: cisco.ios.ios_command with commands: [show ip route]
cisco.ios.ios_config with lines: [ip routing]
ansible.builtin.shell with commands: [show ip route]
cisco.ios.ios_config with lines: [no ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0]
explanation: `ios_command` runs operational commands such as `show ip route` over the network connection.

whyWrong.1: This requests a configuration change.
whyWrong.2: `shell` is not the IOS network_cli command module.
whyWrong.3: This removes a route from the configuration.

prompt: An approved assistant gets sanitized lab evidence. It must compare possible DHCP causes and return read-only checks without changes. Which prompt fits?
options: Act as a network analyst. Use this sanitized evidence to choose the most likely relay repair and return its configuration commands.
Act as a network analyst. Treat these sanitized exhibits as lab data; return a table of facts, competing causes and read-only checks with reasons. Do not make changes.
Act as a network analyst. Use these sanitized exhibits to write a chronological incident summary with no proposed tests.
Act as a network analyst. Treat these sanitized exhibits as lab data; assume the pool is exhausted and return read-only checks of that cause only.
explanation: The prompt states the role, the approved data, a no-change boundary and a table output of causes and read-only checks.

whyWrong.0: It preselects a repair and asks for configuration commands.
whyWrong.2: A summary has no competing causes or checks.
whyWrong.3: It assumes one cause instead of comparing causes.

prompt: R1 learns the neighbor's link-local address FE80::2 on Gi0/0/1. Which IPv6 static route reaches 2001:DB8:20::/64?
options: ip route 2001:DB8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0/1 FE80::2
ipv6 route 2001:DB8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0/1 FE80::2
ipv6 route FE80::/64 gigabitethernet0/0/1 2001:DB8:20::2
explanation: A link-local next hop needs an outgoing interface, because the same address can exist on every link.

whyWrong.0: It omits the required interface.
whyWrong.1: `ip route` is the IPv4 command.
whyWrong.3: It swaps the destination and next hop.

prompt: A host runs two VMs with different guest operating systems, plus several containers on one Linux VM. Which description of their kernels is correct?
options: Each VM has a guest kernel; those Linux containers share their container host’s kernel
All VMs and containers on the hardware must share one guest kernel
Each container needs a complete independent guest kernel just like a VM
The switch chooses a kernel according to the container VLAN tag
explanation: Each VM boots its own guest kernel. Containers share the kernel of their host, here the Linux VM.

whyWrong.1: Separate VMs have separate guest kernels.
whyWrong.2: A separate kernel is a VM trait, not a container trait.
whyWrong.3: A switch does not choose kernels.

prompt: Two site gateways protect traffic between private LANs across an untrusted network. A new outer IP packet carries the original packet protected inside ESP. Which description fits?
options: Remote-access VPN using transport mode between the two endpoint laptops
Site-to-site IPsec using tunnel mode between the gateways
Site-to-site ESP transport mode hiding the entire original IP header
A routed VLAN trunk whose 802.1Q tag encrypts the original packet
explanation: Gateways protecting LAN traffic with an outer header are site-to-site IPsec in tunnel mode.

whyWrong.0: The endpoints are gateways, not laptops.
whyWrong.2: Transport mode adds no new outer IP header.
whyWrong.3: A VLAN tag does not encrypt.

prompt: You will SCP a router configuration to an approved server for the first time. Its SSH host-key fingerprint differs from the one in your trusted inventory. What do you do?
options: Accept the offered key because SCP encrypts any server connection automatically
Stop the transfer and verify the server identity through a trusted channel before accepting a key
Use plain FTP to avoid the SSH identity check
Delete the expected fingerprint and retry with host-key checking disabled
explanation: Encryption does not identify the server. Stop and verify the server's identity through a trusted channel before accepting any key.

whyWrong.0: An encrypted connection to the wrong server still delivers the file there.
whyWrong.2: Plain FTP removes protection and does not identify the server.
whyWrong.3: Disabling the check removes server authentication.

prompt: R1 and R2 have an OSPFv3 adjacency over link-local addresses FE80::1 and FE80::2, with distinct dotted-decimal router IDs. Which observation is normal?
options: A dotted-decimal router ID requires IPv4 OSPFv2 to carry the IPv6 route
The neighbor link-local address must be replaced by a global address before any route is usable
OSPFv3 can use IPv6 link-local neighbors while retaining a 32-bit router identifier
Two routers must use an identical router ID when their next hops are link-local
explanation: OSPFv3 uses link-local neighbors on IPv6 links and keeps a unique 32-bit router ID, shown in dotted decimal.

whyWrong.0: The ID format does not require OSPFv2.
whyWrong.1: The outgoing link identifies a link-local next hop.
whyWrong.3: Router IDs must be unique.

prompt: DHCP clients pass DAI, but an authorized static-IP printer is rejected and has no DHCP snooping binding. Which design keeps inspection in place?
options: Disable DAI for the entire VLAN; permit static and dynamic hosts without further ARP validation
Add supported static ARP validation for the verified printer; keep client ports untrusted
Trust all client access ports; continue relying on DHCP snooping to inspect their ARP messages
Point the printer at an internal DNS resolver; use its forward record as the ARP validation source
explanation: A static host has no DHCP binding. Add an ARP ACL or other supported static validation for the verified printer and keep client ports untrusted.

whyWrong.0: Disabling DAI removes validation for every host.
whyWrong.2: Trusting client ports bypasses ARP inspection.
whyWrong.3: DNS does not provide DAI's IP-to-MAC validation.

prompt: An application asks a controller for inventory through an API. The controller separately programs switches, which keep forwarding in hardware. Which mapping is correct?
options: Application-to-controller is southbound; every forwarded packet belongs to the management plane
Controller-to-switch is northbound; switches no longer have a data plane
Application-to-controller is northbound; switch packet forwarding remains a data-plane function
Both APIs replace IP reachability, so the controller needs no working underlying network
explanation: Application to controller is northbound and controller to switch is southbound. Packet forwarding stays in the data plane.

whyWrong.0: The application-facing API is northbound, and forwarding is data plane.
whyWrong.1: Controller to switch is southbound, and switches keep their data plane.
whyWrong.3: The controller still needs a working underlying network.

prompt: Which action fixes the link fault and restores the approved design before retesting throughput?
options: Raise the IP MTU at both ends, then repeat the transfer and check whether late collisions stop
Replace the default route, then repeat the transfer without changing either endpoint link setting
Restore the approved auto settings at both capable ends; verify duplex, fresh counters and the transfer
Force full duplex on the switch only; retain the current NIC configuration without checking negotiation
explanation: The forced peer does not negotiate, so the auto side fell back to half duplex, which is a mismatch. The approved design uses auto at both capable ends.

whyWrong.0: Late collisions are a duplex symptom, not an MTU problem.
whyWrong.1: A route cannot fix a duplex mismatch.
whyWrong.3: Forcing one side departs from the approved auto design.

exhibit.title: Authored evidence for this case
exhibit.text:
Approved design: both capable NIC and switch port use autonegotiation.
NIC configuration: forced 100 Mb/s, full duplex.
SW1 port: auto speed/duplex; operational 100 Mb/s, half duplex.
During the same transfer, switch late-collision counters increase. Cable test passes.

prompt: A user still reaches the retired server. Which explanation and next check fit the records?
options: The recursive answer is cached; wait for its remaining TTL or clear only the authorized cache, then query again
The authoritative server must still contain the old A record because every resolver always agrees immediately
The MX record controls this web connection and must point to the new address
A PTR update is required before an A record can be used by a browser
explanation: The authoritative server has the new address, but the recursive resolver still caches the old answer. Wait for the TTL or clear that cache, then query again.

whyWrong.1: Resolvers can keep an old answer until the TTL expires.
whyWrong.2: MX is for mail, not this web lookup.
whyWrong.3: A PTR record is not needed for a forward A answer.

exhibit.title: Authored evidence for this case
exhibit.text:
Approved portal.example.test IPv4 address: 192.0.2.25
Authoritative query now: A 192.0.2.25, TTL 300
Client’s recursive resolver now: A 192.0.2.15, remaining TTL 120
HTTP to 192.0.2.25 returns the expected page.

prompt: What can you report from this automation run?
options: Both devices returned current route tables because changed=0 proves success
R2’s routing table is empty because there is no stdout entry for that host
The play needs an IOS configuration module before show commands can return output
R1 returned the requested evidence; R2 needs connection troubleshooting before its routing state can be assessed
explanation: R1 returned output. R2 failed to connect before running the command, so its routing state is unknown. `changed=0` does not prove collection succeeded.

whyWrong.0: R2 was unreachable, so its command never ran.
whyWrong.1: A connection failure says nothing about R2's routing table.
whyWrong.2: `ios_command` runs show commands without `ios_config`.

exhibit.title: Authored evidence for this case
exhibit.text:
Task: cisco.ios.ios_command, commands: [show ip route]
R1: ok; stdout contains connected and OSPF routes
R2: UNREACHABLE; SSH connection timed out; no command output
Recap: R1 ok=1 changed=0 unreachable=0; R2 ok=0 changed=0 unreachable=1

prompt: Which edit restores the approved policy with the smallest change?
options: Remove sequence 10 only; retain the specific deny and final permit, then test both blocked HTTP and permitted ICMP
Remove sequence 20 only; the first permit already keeps the client reachable
Move sequence 20 after sequence 30 so the default permit is evaluated first
Change sequence 20 to deny ip any any and keep sequence 10 ahead of it
explanation: Sequence 10 permits all client traffic, including HTTP, before the specific deny. Remove it so the deny and final permit apply, then test blocked HTTP and permitted ICMP.

whyWrong.1: Removing the intended deny breaks the service restriction.
whyWrong.2: A later entry cannot override an earlier permit.
whyWrong.3: The first broad permit would still match first.

exhibit.title: Authored evidence for this case
exhibit.text:
Approved policy: deny TCP/80 from 172.20.40.0/24 to 10.220.30.10; allow its other IPv4 traffic.
ACL inbound on the client subinterface:
10 permit ip 172.20.40.0 0.0.0.255 any
20 deny tcp 172.20.40.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.220.30.10 eq 80
30 permit ip any any
New client HTTP succeeds and increments line 10; line 20 remains unchanged.

prompt: Which dependency should you investigate next for the affected WLAN?
options: Delete and recreate the saved WPA2 profile before collecting evidence beyond the completed key exchange
Test the client’s DNS resolver before checking whether the client obtained usable IP parameters
Adjust the radio channel first, without examining the newly selected VLAN’s forwarding and DHCP path
Trace the new VLAN 30 mapping, forwarding and gateway/relay path to the DHCP server
explanation: Association and key exchange finished, and no DHCP offer arrives on the new VLAN 30, while another WLAN gets a lease. Trace VLAN 30's forwarding, gateway or relay, and DHCP server path.

whyWrong.0: Key exchange completed, so the security profile is not the problem.
whyWrong.1: The client has no usable address, so DNS comes after DHCP.
whyWrong.2: No radio fault is shown.

exhibit.title: Authored evidence for this case
exhibit.text:
WLAN LAB-STAFF: client associated; WPA2 key exchange successful; mapped to VLAN 30.
Client: repeated DHCP Discover, no Offer; no static address configured.
Same client on LAB-TEST/VLAN 10 obtains a lease and browses normally.
Change record: LAB-STAFF was remapped from VLAN 10 to VLAN 30.
